title: Mongols
wiki_lead:
The Mongols are an East Asian ethnic group native to Mongolia and China (Inner Mongolia and other 11 autonomous territories), as well as parts of southern Siberia. The Mongols are the principal member of the large family of Mongolic peoples. The Oirats and the Buryats are classified either as distinct ethno-linguistic groups or as subgroups of Mongols.
The Mongols are bound together by a common heritage and ethnic identity, descending from the Proto-Mongols. Their indigenous dialects are collectively known as the Mongolian language. The contiguous geographical area in which the Mongols primarily live is referred to as the Mongol heartland, especially in discussions of the Mongols' history under the Mongol Empire and Northern Yuan.

The Mongols are an East Asian ethnic group native to Mongolia and China (Inner Mongolia and other 11 autonomous territories), as well as parts of southern Siberia. The Mongols are the principal member of the large family of Mongolic peoples. The Oirats and the Buryats are classified either as distinct ethno-linguistic groups or as subgroups of Mongols.
The Mongols are bound together by a common heritage and ethnic identity, descending from the Proto-Mongols. Their indigenous dialects are collectively known as the Mongolian language. The contiguous geographical area in which the Mongols primarily live is referred to as the Mongol heartland, especially in discussions of the Mongols' history under the Mongol Empire and Northern Yuan.


Etymology

There are several proposals for the etymology of the ethnonym "Mongol":

A change from Mongkhe-tengri-gal ("Eternal Sky Fire");
A derivation from the personal name, transcribed in Chinese-language sources as 木骨閭 Mùgǔlǘ (from Middle Chinese *muwk-kwot-ljo), of the progenitor of the Rouran Khaganate.
The designation "Mongol" first appeared in the mid-10th century Chinese Old Book of Tang to describe a tribe of the Shiwei who resided in the Argun River basin in the 9th century. In the 13th century, the word Mongol grew into an umbrella term for a large group of Mongolic-speaking tribes united under the rule of Genghis Khan.
The Mongols of the Mongol Empire were known in Central Asia, Western Asia and Europe as "Tatars", after a tribal confederation that was active on the Mongolian Steppes in the 12th century.


History


Prehistoric background

The ethnogenesis of Mongolic peoples is largely linked with the expansion of Ancient Northeast Asians. The Mongolian pastoralist lifestyle may in part be derived from the Western Steppe Herders, but without much geneflow between these two groups, suggesting cultural transmission.


Early historical background
In various times Mongolic peoples have been equated with the Scythians, the Magog, and the Tungusic peoples. Based on Chinese historical texts the ancestry of the Mongolic peoples can be traced back to the Donghu, a nomadic confederation occupying eastern Mongolia and Manchuria. The Donghu neighboured the Xiongnu, whose identity is still debated today. Although some scholars maintain that they were proto-Mongols, they were more likely a multi-ethnic group of Mongolic and Turkic tribes. It has been suggested that the language of the Huns was related to the Xiongnu.
The Donghu, however, can be much more easily labeled proto-Mongol since the Chinese histories trace only Mongolic tribes and kingdoms (Xianbei and Wuhuan peoples) from them, although some historical texts claim a mixed Xiongnu-Donghu ancestry for some tribes (e.g. the Khitan).

grok_lead: The Mongols are an East Asian ethnic group native to the steppes of the Mongolian Plateau, historically defined by their nomadic pastoralism centered on herding livestock such as horses, sheep, and goats, which shaped their mobile, warrior society. Primarily consisting of subgroups like the Khalkha, they form the majority ethnic population in Mongolia, accounting for approximately 85% of its inhabitants, with significant communities in China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region and parts of Russia. Originating from ancient nomadic confederations traceable to Bronze Age Slab Grave cultures and Iron Age Xiongnu populations on the Mongolian steppe, the Mongols achieved unification under TemÃ¼jin around 1206, when he was proclaimed Genghis Khan and formed the Khamag Mongol Ulus (All Mongol State) by subjugating rival tribes through alliances, warfare, and merit-based leadership. This consolidation enabled rapid expansion, leveraging superior cavalry tactics including feigned retreats, encirclement maneuvers, and composite bow archery from horseback, which emphasized mobility, deception, and coordinated unit discipline over static fortifications. The resulting Mongol Empire, at its peak in the mid- 13th century, spanned from Eastern Europe and the Persian Gulf to the Pacific Ocean, incorporating diverse territories through relentless conquests that integrated conquered engineers for siege warfare and promoted trade via the Pax Mongolica, fostering exchanges of technologies, goods, and ideas across Eurasia despite the immense human costs of the campaigns. Key achievements included administrative innovations like the yam relay postal system for communication, religious tolerance under the yassa legal code, and patronage of arts and scholarship during the Yuan Dynasty in China under Kublai Khan, Genghis's grandson, though the empire fragmented into khanates amid internal strife and overextension by the late 13th century. Modern Mongols, numbering around 10 million globally, retain cultural elements like eagle hunting and naadam festivals, while navigating post-communist transitions in Mongolia and ethnic tensions in China.
